query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If a dense oxide coating (e.g., Al2O3 or ZrO2) is deposited via CVD or PVD on boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, then the molten-aluminum corrosion rate will be significantly reduced by creating a stable barrier that inhibits chemical attack and diffusion at 700–750 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based substrate (e.g., Fe2B or a boride-rich cermet) in uncoated form intended for hot-dip aluminum exposure.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a uniform oxide film by CVD or PVD onto the boride-based substrate before service.
generation.conditions: Continuous or batch immersion in molten aluminum at 700–750 °C, typical of hot-dip plating lines; limited oxygen or inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Dense, adherent oxide layer that impedes direct molten aluminum contact and suppresses dissolution of the underlying boride matrix.
generation.mechanism: The chemically stable oxide film lowers interdiffusion and prevents reactive attacks, reducing substrate wear and mass loss from molten aluminum corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an uncoated boride reference, the coated boride-based substrate will exhibit at least a 30–50% lower mass loss and fewer intermetallic reaction layers in cross-section analyses over a 100-hour test.
generation.baseline: Equivalent boride-based component without oxide coating, exposed under the same molten aluminum conditions.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness depends on coating integrity (e.g., free of cracks or delamination) and stability under sustained 700–750 °C operation. Thermal shocks above 750 °C or coating defects can degrade performance.
generation.uncertainty: Long-term adherence under severe thermal cycling and the effect of any plating bath contaminants remain to be thoroughly characterized before large-scale adoption.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based samples—one set coated with an oxide layer, the other uncoated. Immerse both in molten aluminum at 720 °C for 100 hours. Monitor weight change at 25-hour intervals and perform metallographic cross-sections after exposure.
measurements: Mass loss or thickness change measurements
SEM/EDS of cross-sections to evaluate coating integrity and reaction layers
Hardness tests on exposed surfaces to detect localized damage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a noticeably lower mass loss (less than 10% difference) and no reduced intermetallic layer formation compared to uncoated controls, the hypothesis shall be regarded as falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, a reinforced layer was prepared on the surface of HEA by powder-pack boriding and focused on the effect of temperature and duration on the boronizing of CoCrFeNiMn HEA. The boronized samples were characterized using various methods. Furthermore, the properties of boronized CoCrFeNiMn alloys and diffusion behavior were investigated. This study could provide a reference for high hardness and high wear resistance HEA that could be used in a variety of industrial applications, such as the mold and crucible used in the cast aluminum industry [,], because the borides formed on the surface have high hardness, excellent corrosion resistance, and wear resistance [,], which allow HEA to be applied in special environments to increase service life.

In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.
